# Organize Your Photos with Apple Intelligence: Smart Search & Editing

Imagine typing "my dog running on the beach" and seeing exactly those photos, without scrolling through years of pictures. With Apple Intelligence in the Photos app on your iPhone, you can search by describing what you want to find, and you can remove a stranger or a trash can from the background with the Clean Up tool. One honest note before you start: Apple Intelligence does not sharpen a blurry photo. Clean Up removes distracting objects; it does not bring an out-of-focus shot back into focus.

## Before you start
- **A supported iPhone:** an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, or iPhone 16 model or later, with Apple Intelligence turned on.
- **A supported language:** Apple Intelligence works when your Siri and device language are set to a supported language, such as English or Spanish. It is not available in all languages or regions, and Clean Up has its own region and language limits.
- **Some photos in your library**, ideally with a few you'd like to find quickly.
- **About 10 minutes.** Apple notes that some photo editing tools have daily usage limits.

## Step 1 — Open search in the Photos app
Go to the **Photos** app and tap the **Search** button (the magnifying glass) in the bottom-right corner. You can search the whole library, or open a specific album or collection first and search inside it.

You'll know it worked when the search field opens and Photos shows suggestions of dates, locations, and people you've named in your library.

💬 Example: tap **Search** and look at the suggestions before you type anything — they're built from your own library.

## Step 2 — Search by date, place, or category
Type what you're looking for into the search field. Photos understands a date (a month or year), a place (a city or state), a business name, a category (like beach or sunset), an event (like a concert), a person or pet you've named, text in a photo (like a phone number), or a caption. Tap one of the suggestions, or tap the search key on the keyboard.

You'll know it worked when matching photos appear; swipe up to browse the complete results.

💬 Example: type `sunset` or `July 2025`.

## Step 3 — Describe the photo in your own words
With Apple Intelligence you don't have to think in keywords. Type a description in natural language, the way you'd explain the picture to a friend. Apple's own examples are "Maya skateboarding in a tie-dye shirt" and "Sadie cartwheeling on the grass". You can also search video clips for key moments.

You'll know it worked when the results show the specific scene you described rather than every photo of that person or place.

💬 Example: type `my dog running on the beach` — use your pet's name if you've named it in Photos.

## Step 4 — Narrow down, sort, and collect the results
Once you have results, you can tidy them up:
- **Sort:** tap the sort button, then **Added** (date added to your library) or **Captured** (date taken).
- **Filter:** tap the filter button, then an option such as **Favorites** or **Edited**.
- **Narrow by type:** add a media type to your search, such as **Video** or **Portrait**.
- **See related albums and memories:** tap **Collections**.
- **Keep them together:** tap **Select**, choose the photos you want, then share them or add them to an album.

You'll know it worked when the list is short enough to scan at a glance, or your chosen photos are in an album.

💬 Example: search `birthday`, add `Video` to the search, then tap **Select** and add the clips to an album called "Birthday 2026".

## Step 5 — Remove a distraction with Clean Up
Open a photo and tap the **Edit** button. Tap **Tools**, then tap **Clean Up**. Now tap, brush, or circle what you want to remove; some items may already be highlighted so you can remove them with a single tap. Pinch with two fingers to zoom or pan for small objects. If you're using High Quality processing, tap **Clean Up** to apply it. Save your edit, then tap **Done** to close the photo.

You can choose how Photos processes Clean Up — **Auto**, **Fast**, or **High Quality** — by tapping **Auto** during the Clean Up process.

You'll know it worked when the object is gone and the background fills in where it was.

💬 Example: circle a person walking through the background of a holiday photo.

## Step 6 — Undo Clean Up if you change your mind
Your original isn't lost. To undo Clean Up after saving, open the photo again, tap **Edit**, tap **Tools**, then tap **Reset**.

You'll know it worked when the removed object is back in the photo.

💬 Example: if the filled-in background looks smudged, reset it, zoom in, and try again with a smaller brush stroke.

## Common mistakes
- **Expecting Apple Intelligence to fix blur.** Clean Up removes objects; it does not sharpen an out-of-focus or shaky photo. If a photo matters, take a second shot on the spot.
- **Searching with one vague word.** "Dog" returns every dog photo. A short description — who, what, where — gets you to the right picture much faster.
- **Passing off an edited photo as untouched.** In iOS 27.2 or later, most images created or edited with Apple Intelligence tools include a hidden SynthID watermark that shows they were changed with generative tools. If a photo matters as a record (an insurance claim, a listing), keep the original.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** You can find "grandma's birthday cake" or "the kids at the lake" in seconds, and remove a photobomber before you share the picture with family.
- **For your business or work:** Pull every photo of a product or a site visit by describing it, collect them in one album, and clean up stray clutter in the background of a quick product shot.
- **If you're just getting started:** Begin with search — it changes nothing in your library. Try Clean Up first on a photo that doesn't matter much.

## Try it now
Open **Photos**, tap **Search** in the bottom-right corner, and type a description of one photo you remember — for example, `me holding a fish at the lake`. Then open the best result, tap **Edit → Tools → Clean Up**, and remove one small distraction.
